title: Prohibited communications and other rules
blurb: Know where spread spectrum is allowed, what Line A restricts, what you may not send for money, and how amplifier certification works.

E1F01.why: Spread spectrum is permitted only on amateur frequencies **above 222 MHz**.
E1F01.trap: The limit is 222 MHz exactly, not 50, 144 or 420.

E1F02.why: A Canadian licensee operates by the **terms of the Canadian license**, never above US Amateur Extra privileges.

E1F03.why: A dealer may sell an uncertified amplifier that was **bought used from an amateur** and sold to another amateur for use at their station.
E1F03.trap: Kit assembly, foreign certification and low gain are not exceptions.

E1F04.why: Line A lies roughly **parallel to and south of** the US-Canada border.

E1F05.why: North of Line A in the contiguous 48 states, **420 to 430 MHz** is off limits.

E1F06.why: The FCC may issue an STA for **experimental amateur communications**.
E1F06.trap: An STA does not bridge upgrade posting delays or short VE teams.

E1F07.why: Messages to a business are legal only when **neither you nor your employer** has a pecuniary interest. No dollar threshold applies.

E1F08.why: Communications **for hire or material compensation** are prohibited, except as the rules provide.
E1F08.trap: Other languages and religious content are not what is prohibited.

E1F09.why: Messages **encoded to obscure their meaning** are prohibited on any amateur network. Email and third-party traffic are not.

E1F10.why: An auxiliary station's control operator must be **Technician, General, Advanced or Amateur Extra**.

E1F11.why: A certified amplifier must satisfy the FCC **spurious emission standards** at the lesser of **1500 W** or its full output.
E1F11.trap: Gain figures and UL listing are not the standard.
